description: We are a team of six passionate and motivated students participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Our project, **RotaSat**, aims to transform NASA satellite data into practical agricultural solutions by helping farmers make more informed and sustainable crop rotation decisions. We are developing a digital platform that analyzes climate conditions, soil health, water availability, and agricultural risks, complemented by an IoT prototype that uses sensors to monitor soil conditions.
summary:
Sowlt is a farmer-centered decision-support application developed for Cuatro Cañadas, Santa Cruz, Bolivia, a major soybean-producing region facing recurring droughts, extreme rainfall, and progressive soil degradation. To address the Field Shift challenge, we built a mobile-first platform powered by a deterministic, explainable agronomic engine that harmonizes NASA POWER meteorological reanalysis and NASA GIBS satellite layers with local crop parameters, FAO-56 Penman-Monteith reference evapotranspiration (ET0), soil constraints, and user-weighted priorities.

Rather than relying on opaque black-box predictions, Sowlt evaluates and compares four 12-month crop-rotation strategies: the farmer's baseline alongside soil-conservation, water-efficiency, and balanced alternatives, using Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) and 200-iteration climate-year bootstrapping (P10–P90 intervals). Each option explicitly communicates selection rationale, traceable NASA evidence, agronomic trade-offs, information gaps, and targeted questions for local agronomists. Complemented by a calibrated three-zone ESP32 soil-sensing node and physics-based digital twin demonstrating sub-pixel field heterogeneity against coarse regional satellite grids, Sowlt empowers producers to make climate-resilient rotation decisions while reinforcing, rather than replacing, local agricultural expertise.
details:
Sowlt: NASA-Powered Agricultural Decision Support for Cuatro Cañadas, Santa Cruz, Bolivia

What does it do and how does it work?

Sowlt is a farmer-centered, mobile-first decision-support application developed for Cuatro Cañadas, Santa Cruz, Bolivia (reference point: -17.2374, -62.2427). The region is a major grain and oilseed area dominated by summer soybean, with winter rotations of sorghum, maize, sunflower, and wheat.

Through a five-question conversational interface with Spanish crop-synonym normalization, the farmer enters the current crop, the previous crop or fallow period, irrigation status, field notes, and core priority (saving water, protecting soil, reducing risk, or balancing all three).

Instead of an opaque black-box machine learning model, Sowlt runs a deterministic, auditable agro-meteorological pipeline:

  1. Earth observation ingestion and harmonization. The backend ingests and caches daily NASA POWER series (2015-2025 historical baseline plus 2026 observations) and hourly series. The variables are T2M, T2M_MAX, T2M_MIN, PRECTOTCORR, RH2M, WS2M, ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN, and GWETROOT. It integrates verified satellite tile layers from NASA GIBS (WMTS) and supports optional adapters for SMAP L4, GPM IMERG, and MODIS/VIIRS NDVI. Daily series are aggregated into local summer and winter cropping windows, and each metric is explicitly tagged with its spatial scale (e.g., ~50 km regional context).
    • FAO-56 Penman-Monteith reference evapotranspiration (ET0)
    • Crop water demand (ETc = Kc × ET0)
    • Empirical effective rainfall (Pef)
    • Seasonal water balance (Pef − ETc)
    • Maximum consecutive dry days (CDD)
    • Seasonal rainfall anomalies
    • Crop-specific heat-stress days
    • Extreme rainfall days (> P95)
    • E0: Current rotation
    • E1: Soil-first
    • E2: Water-first
    • E3: Balanced (maximin)
  2. Actionable explainability and geospatial/field views. Every strategy card outputs five structured blocks: selection rationale, traceable evidence (source, date, unit, scale), trade-offs, missing information, and targeted questions for local agronomists. The app also includes a five-layer geospatial viewer and a Field Data module linked to an ESP32 three-zone soil sensor node.

What benefits does it offer?

  • Accessible decision support in under three minutes. It translates complex satellite datasets and evapotranspiration physics into a plain, high-contrast Spanish interface for mobile use in the field, with no geospatial expertise required.
  • Full scientific traceability. Every number carries a strict provenance label: documented, derived, assumption, farmer_provided, unavailable, or simulated. Because the system uses an explainable rule-based and MCDA engine rather than unvalidated predictive or generative models, every recommendation can be audited back to raw NASA observations and FAO-56 equations, with no risk of model hallucination.
  • Interactive sensitivity exploration. NASA data ingestion is decoupled from decision scoring, so farmers can adjust priority sliders (Water, Soil, Risk) in real time and immediately see how strategy rankings and trade-offs shift.
  • Explicit uncertainty and data-gap transparency. Sowlt issues no yield guarantees. It visualizes historical climate variability (P10-P90), caps the confidence rating when local soil analyses are absent, and converts missing variables into concrete questions for local extension technicians.

What is the intended impact?

In Santa Cruz, recurring droughts, soil fertility loss, and extreme rainfall events have affected 5,138 farming families, damaged or destroyed 330,000 hectares, and generated an estimated USD 190 million in projected losses. In Cuatro Cañadas (318,083 ha of soybean in 2023), these pressures have forced producers to abruptly abandon winter crops such as wheat in favor of sorghum.

Sowlt is designed to help producers break soil-degrading cycles and adapt winter planting decisions to shifting water availability, without treating agriculture as a gamble. By structuring evidence and highlighting local blind spots, it strengthens collaboration among farmers, agricultural associations (such as ANAPO), and local agronomists.

Its decoupled architecture separates the NASA data pipeline from localized JSON crop and rule bases. This allows rapid scaling to other municipalities across Bolivia and Latin America.

What tools, programming languages, hardware, and software were used?

  • Backend and scientific computing: Python 3.11+, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic v2, NumPy, pandas, SciPy (nonlinear curve fitting for sensor calibration), requests, jsonschema, pytest, and SQLite (field-node telemetry storage).
    • Firmware and simulation: C++ / Arduino framework (Arduino IDE 2 / PlatformIO) and Wokwi (virtual ESP32 circuit and firmware simulation).
    • Sensors and microcontroller: ESP32 DevKit, 3× capacitive soil moisture sensors (v1.2), 3× waterproof DS18B20 temperature probes (1-Wire bus), BME680 environmental sensor (I2C: temperature, relative humidity, barometric pressure, gas resistance), DHT11 (quality-control redundancy), and a GL55xx LDR photoresistor.
    • Connectivity: cloudflared / ngrok for HTTPS tunneling.
  • Datasets and agronomic reference standards: NASA POWER REST API, NASA GIBS WMTS, FAO-56 Crop Evapotranspiration (Penman-Monteith and Kc tables), FAO Effective Rainfall methodology, FAO EcoCrop database, and municipal agricultural statistics from Bolivia’s MDPYEP/INE.

How is the project creative?

  • Explainable MCDA with climate-year bootstrapping. Rather than forcing generative AI or supervised ML onto a region that lacks labeled multi-year, farm-level yield datasets, we designed a transparent mathematical decision engine. It pairs multi-criteria scoring with 200-run historical climate bootstrapping to quantify how stable a rotation choice is across wet and dry years.
    • Bucket soil-water balance
    • Damped sinusoidal soil heat diffusion
    • LDR voltage-divider response
    • Sensor fault injection
  • Tangible demonstration of sub-pixel heterogeneity. Sensors are deployed across three soil moisture zones (dry, medium, wet) and contrasted with regional NASA POWER (~50 km) and SMAP (~9 km) context. This physically shows farmers why coarse satellite pixels average out localized field variability.
  • Lightweight isometric “mission terminal” layer stack. In the geospatial viewer, five environmental layers (rainfall, soil moisture, heat, vegetation, water balance) are rendered over Leaflet using hardware-accelerated CSS 3D transforms (rotateX / rotateZ) instead of a heavy 3D engine. This preserves performance on low-end mobile devices.

What factors did our team consider?

  • Spatial and temporal scale honesty. We strictly avoided presenting coarse ~50 km reanalysis cells as field-level measurements. Every metric in the UI displays its native spatial resolution, observation timestamp, and temporal aggregation window.
    • A three-point gravimetric calibration protocol for each capacitive probe (wet-to-dry mass ratio multiplied by bulk density)
    • Ice/water-bath offset calibration for the DS18B20 probes
    • 64-sample averaging, strictly on ESP32 ADC1 pins (avoiding ADC2 dropouts when Wi-Fi is active)
    • Bland-Altman agreement checks between the BME680 and DHT11
  • Rural connectivity and farmer accessibility. Anticipating intermittent rural internet, we implemented local caching of NASA POWER series on the backend and circular offline buffering in the ESP32 firmware. The mobile-first UI uses ≥ 16 px typography, dual icon-and-text status indicators (never relying on color alone), and local Bolivian Spanish phrasing.
